item.title: How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds
item.dc:creator: Shalma Wegsman
item.description:
The artist had no formal math education, yet as a new exhibition shows, the insights revealed in his artwork became an enduring inspiration to mathematicians.

The post How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds first appeared on Quanta Magazine
item.content:encoded:
Maurits Cornelis Escher didn’t plan on becoming the darling of mathematicians. Born in 1898 in the canal-lined city of Leeuwarden in the Netherlands, Escher struggled with mathematics as a student, once remarking that he “never got a pass mark.” He ended up studying decorative arts and printmaking, and he used his artwork to explore the strange rules of nature that he found operating around him.

item.dc:creator: Charlie Wood
item.description:
An era-defining galaxy survey has released its final results. They don’t quite fit the leading theory of cosmology.

item.title: Can Network Science Transform Health and Nutrition?
item.dc:creator: Steven Strogatz and Janna Levin
item.description:
Albert-László Barabási explains how the same organizing principles shape everything from the internet to the cell, and how mapping the networks inside our bodies could change how we treat disease and think about food.

item.content:encoded:
Nothing really exists in isolation. Almost every part of our lives exists in a network. Consciousness arises from what neurons do together, life from what genes and proteins do together, society from what we do together.
